content.text: I have enough now to compile a comprehensive, well-organized survey of organizations across the AI industry's load-bearing categories.

input.summary: The organizations facet spans five clusters a daily reader meets constantly: (1) frontier builders — a small set of labs (US, and increasingly Chinese) shipping the models that set the pace; (2) infrastructure — chipmakers, foundries, and hyperscaler clouds whose supply constraints and capex now drive the news cycle as much as model releases; (3) capital — the VC firms and sovereign wealth vehicles writing the mega-rounds that fund frontier training runs; (4) governance — the patchwork of national institutes, regulators, and standards bodies now moving from voluntary frameworks to binding enforcement (EU AI Act enforcement began August 2026); (5) research and evaluation — nonprofits, academic labs, and open-source collectives that produce the benchmarks, safety evals, and open-weight alternatives the rest of the ecosystem cites. Corporate structures matter here (OpenAI's nonprofit/PBC split, Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, Google DeepMind's absorption into Alphabet) and several entities have recently renamed or repositioned (UK AISI → AI Security Institute; US AISI → CAISI), so canonical current names are flagged where a rename occurred.

items.name: OpenAI
items.detail: Creator of GPT and ChatGPT; operates under a capped-profit structure (OpenAI Global, LLC) controlled by the OpenAI nonprofit foundation, with Microsoft as its largest strategic partner/investor.

items.name: Anthropic
items.detail: Builder of the Claude model family; a public benefit corporation founded by ex-OpenAI researchers, governed in part by an independent Long-Term Benefit Trust; major backers include Google and Amazon.

items.name: Google DeepMind
items.detail: Alphabet's unified AI research and product lab (merger of Google Brain and DeepMind, completed 2023), builder of the Gemini model family and TPU-adjacent research.

items.name: xAI
items.detail: Elon Musk's AI lab, builder of the Grok model family, now merged with X (Twitter) under Musk's holding structure; experienced high-profile leadership departures in early 2026.

items.name: Meta AI (FAIR / Meta Superintelligence Labs)
items.detail: Meta Platforms' AI division, historically known for open-weight Llama releases and FAIR (Fundamental AI Research); restructured into Meta Superintelligence Labs amid a stalled flagship model in 2026.

items.name: Mistral AI
items.detail: Paris-based frontier lab and Europe's leading open-weight and commercial model builder (Mistral Large/Medium/Small families), positioned as the EU's sovereign-AI champion.

items.name: Nvidia
items.detail: Dominant AI accelerator (GPU) maker and CUDA software ecosystem owner; its supply, pricing, and roadmap (Blackwell, Rubin) function as an industry-wide pacing signal.

items.name: DeepSeek
items.detail: Hangzhou-based Chinese lab (High-Flyer-backed) whose efficient open-weight DeepSeek-V3/R1 releases reset assumptions about training cost and triggered market-wide reaction in early 2025.

items.name: Alibaba (Qwen)
items.detail: Alibaba Cloud's Qwen model family is one of the most widely adopted open-weight series globally, anchoring China's open-source AI push.

items.name: Moonshot AI
items.detail: Chinese lab behind the Kimi model family; released Kimi K2/K3 as among the largest open-weight models, competing aggressively on cost and long-context/coding performance.

items.name: Zhipu AI (Z.ai)
items.detail: Chinese lab behind the GLM model family, strong in enterprise and Chinese-language applications; rebranded consumer-facing products under the Z.ai name.

items.name: Baidu
items.detail: Chinese search giant and builder of the ERNIE model family; longstanding enterprise and Chinese-market AI incumbent.

items.name: ByteDance (Doubao / Seed)
items.detail: TikTok's parent company, builder of the Doubao consumer assistant and Seed research models; a major but less internationally visible Chinese frontier player.

items.name: Microsoft
items.detail: OpenAI's largest investor and cloud/compute partner (Azure); also ships its own Copilot product line and MAI in-house model research.

items.name: Amazon (AWS / Amazon AI)
items.detail: Major cloud provider and Anthropic investor; builds custom AI silicon (Trainium/Inferentia) and the Bedrock/Nova model platforms.

items.name: Apple
items.detail: Ships on-device and cloud AI (Apple Intelligence) with a privacy-emphasizing architecture; a comparatively slower-moving frontier participant but a major distribution channel via iOS.

items.name: AMD
items.detail: Nvidia's primary GPU/accelerator challenger (MI300/MI400 series, Helios racks); anchored by a large multi-year OpenAI compute deal disclosed in 2025-2026.

items.name: Broadcom
items.detail: Critical custom-silicon design partner for hyperscaler AI ASICs, including Google's TPUs and OpenAI's in-house accelerator program; a key but less consumer-visible infrastructure gatekeeper.

items.name: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)
items.detail: Sole leading-edge foundry for nearly all frontier AI chips (Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Broadcom, Google); its CoWoS packaging capacity is a binding industry-wide constraint.

items.name: Intel
items.detail: Legacy chipmaker attempting an AI accelerator comeback (Gaudi line) and foundry pivot; a much smaller AI-compute player than Nvidia/AMD/TSMC but strategically watched for US chip-sovereignty reasons.

items.name: CoreWeave
items.detail: GPU-cloud specialist ('neocloud') that became a major AI infrastructure provider by renting Nvidia capacity at scale to labs including OpenAI and Microsoft.

items.name: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) / CAISI
items.detail: US government standards body; its AI Safety Institute was renamed the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in 2025, shifting emphasis toward standards, security, and countering foreign over-regulation rather than broad safety framing.

items.name: UK AI Security Institute (AISI)
items.detail: UK government body (formerly named the AI Safety Institute; renamed AI Security Institute in Feb 2025) that evaluates frontier models for national-security-relevant risks; publishes active technical safety research.

items.name: European AI Office
items.detail: European Commission body that both develops guidance and enforces the EU AI Act's general-purpose-AI obligations; high-risk obligations began applying broadly from August 2026.

items.name: International AI Safety Institute Network
items.detail: Coalition of national AI safety/security institutes (US, UK, EU, Japan, Canada, Australia, Singapore, Korea, and others) launched from the 2023 Bletchley Summit process to coordinate frontier-model evaluation.

items.name: OECD.AI Policy Observatory
items.detail: OECD's AI policy arm; author of the widely cited OECD AI Principles, which underpin much subsequent national and international AI governance vocabulary.

items.name: NVIDIA-adjacent standards: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42
items.detail: The ISO/IEC joint technical committee producing AI management-system standards, notably ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems), increasingly used as an audit/compliance baseline alongside NIST's AI RMF.

items.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
items.detail: Primary US enforcement agency for AI-related consumer protection, deceptive-practice, and competition actions against AI companies, absent a comprehensive federal AI statute.

items.name: California Department of Justice / California AI legislation (e.g., SB 53)
items.detail: California has become a de facto US AI regulator via state law (transparency and safety-disclosure requirements for frontier developers), given federal gridlock.

items.name: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC)
items.detail: China's primary AI/internet regulator, responsible for generative-AI service approvals and content/algorithm registration requirements that all Chinese labs must clear before public release.

items.name: METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research)
items.detail: Berkeley-based nonprofit that runs independent capability and dangerous-capability evaluations on frontier models pre-deployment, frequently cited in lab system cards and government assessments.

items.name: Epoch AI
items.detail: Nonprofit research group tracking compute trends, training-run scale, and model benchmarking data; a widely cited independent data source for the pace of frontier AI progress.

items.name: Apollo Research
items.detail: AI safety organization specializing in evaluating models for deceptive alignment and 'scheming' behavior; has published joint findings with OpenAI on this topic.

items.name: Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)
items.detail: The oldest dedicated AI safety research organization (est. 2000), focused on theoretical alignment and existential-risk research rather than empirical evaluation.

items.name: Center for AI Safety (CAIS)
items.detail: Nonprofit behind the widely signed 2023 'statement on AI risk' and ongoing work on benchmarks (e.g., MMLU-related and safety benchmarks) and AI policy advocacy.

items.name: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2)
items.detail: Seattle nonprofit research lab (founded by Paul Allen) producing fully open models, datasets, and benchmarks (OLMo series); a leading source of open-science alternatives to closed frontier labs.

items.name: Hugging Face
items.detail: The dominant open model/dataset hosting hub and library ecosystem (Transformers, Diffusers); functions as the de facto distribution and discovery layer for open-weight AI.

items.name: EleutherAI
items.detail: Grassroots nonprofit open-research collective (GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, Pythia, the Pile dataset); smaller-budget peer to Ai2 in the open-research ecosystem.

items.name: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) / CRFM
items.detail: Academic policy and research hub best known for the annual AI Index Report, a widely cited benchmark-of-record for industry-wide trends.

items.name: Mila – Quebec AI Institute
items.detail: Montreal-based academic AI research institute (associated with Yoshua Bengio), a leading center for deep learning research and AI-safety-adjacent policy work.

items.name: UK Alan Turing Institute
items.detail: UK's national institute for data science and AI, playing a research and government-advisory role distinct from the AI Security Institute's evaluation mandate.

items.name: Partnership on AI
items.detail: Multi-stakeholder nonprofit coalition (labs, civil society, academia) developing shared norms and best practices around responsible AI deployment.

items.name: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z)
items.detail: Leading venture capital firm with a dedicated AI investment strategy; among the most active backers of foundation-model and applied-AI startups.

items.name: Sequoia Capital
items.detail: Major venture firm with sustained frontier-model and applied-AI investments; participates alongside sovereign wealth funds in mega-rounds.

items.name: Thrive Capital
items.detail: Josh Kushner's venture firm and one of OpenAI's most concentrated institutional backers across multiple funding rounds.

items.name: SoftBank Group
items.detail: Japanese conglomerate and major OpenAI investor/compute-infrastructure partner (Stargate project), representative of sovereign-scale capital entering frontier AI.

items.name: MGX / Gulf sovereign wealth funds (e.g., PIF, Mubadala)
items.detail: Sovereign wealth vehicles (UAE's MGX, Saudi PIF, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala) increasingly co-anchoring mega-rounds and compute infrastructure deals for OpenAI, xAI, and others.

items.name: World Economic Forum (AI Governance Alliance)
items.detail: Convener of cross-industry AI governance dialogue among labs, governments, and civil society; less binding than regulators but agenda-setting for elite consensus.

items.name: UN AI Advisory Body / Global Dialogue on AI Governance
items.detail: United Nations mechanism (following the 2023-24 High-Level Advisory Body on AI) pursuing international coordination on AI governance, distinct from any binding authority.

structured_output.summary: The organizations facet spans five clusters a daily reader meets constantly: (1) frontier builders — a small set of labs (US, and increasingly Chinese) shipping the models that set the pace; (2) infrastructure — chipmakers, foundries, and hyperscaler clouds whose supply constraints and capex now drive the news cycle as much as model releases; (3) capital — the VC firms and sovereign wealth vehicles writing the mega-rounds that fund frontier training runs; (4) governance — the patchwork of national institutes, regulators, and standards bodies now moving from voluntary frameworks to binding enforcement (EU AI Act enforcement began August 2026); (5) research and evaluation — nonprofits, academic labs, and open-source collectives that produce the benchmarks, safety evals, and open-weight alternatives the rest of the ecosystem cites. Corporate structures matter here (OpenAI's nonprofit/PBC split, Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, Google DeepMind's absorption into Alphabet) and several entities have recently renamed or repositioned (UK AISI → AI Security Institute; US AISI → CAISI), so canonical current names are flagged where a rename occurred.

items.name: OpenAI
items.detail: Creator of GPT and ChatGPT; operates under a capped-profit structure (OpenAI Global, LLC) controlled by the OpenAI nonprofit foundation, with Microsoft as its largest strategic partner/investor.

items.name: Anthropic
items.detail: Builder of the Claude model family; a public benefit corporation founded by ex-OpenAI researchers, governed in part by an independent Long-Term Benefit Trust; major backers include Google and Amazon.

items.name: Google DeepMind
items.detail: Alphabet's unified AI research and product lab (merger of Google Brain and DeepMind, completed 2023), builder of the Gemini model family and TPU-adjacent research.

items.name: xAI
items.detail: Elon Musk's AI lab, builder of the Grok model family, now merged with X (Twitter) under Musk's holding structure; experienced high-profile leadership departures in early 2026.

items.name: Meta AI (FAIR / Meta Superintelligence Labs)
items.detail: Meta Platforms' AI division, historically known for open-weight Llama releases and FAIR (Fundamental AI Research); restructured into Meta Superintelligence Labs amid a stalled flagship model in 2026.

items.name: Mistral AI
items.detail: Paris-based frontier lab and Europe's leading open-weight and commercial model builder (Mistral Large/Medium/Small families), positioned as the EU's sovereign-AI champion.

items.name: Nvidia
items.detail: Dominant AI accelerator (GPU) maker and CUDA software ecosystem owner; its supply, pricing, and roadmap (Blackwell, Rubin) function as an industry-wide pacing signal.

items.name: DeepSeek
items.detail: Hangzhou-based Chinese lab (High-Flyer-backed) whose efficient open-weight DeepSeek-V3/R1 releases reset assumptions about training cost and triggered market-wide reaction in early 2025.

items.name: Alibaba (Qwen)
items.detail: Alibaba Cloud's Qwen model family is one of the most widely adopted open-weight series globally, anchoring China's open-source AI push.

items.name: Moonshot AI
items.detail: Chinese lab behind the Kimi model family; released Kimi K2/K3 as among the largest open-weight models, competing aggressively on cost and long-context/coding performance.

items.name: Zhipu AI (Z.ai)
items.detail: Chinese lab behind the GLM model family, strong in enterprise and Chinese-language applications; rebranded consumer-facing products under the Z.ai name.

items.name: Baidu
items.detail: Chinese search giant and builder of the ERNIE model family; longstanding enterprise and Chinese-market AI incumbent.

items.name: Microsoft
items.detail: OpenAI's largest investor and cloud/compute partner (Azure); also ships its own Copilot product line and MAI in-house model research.

items.name: Amazon (AWS / Amazon AI)
items.detail: Major cloud provider and Anthropic investor; builds custom AI silicon (Trainium/Inferentia) and the Bedrock/Nova model platforms.

items.name: Apple
items.detail: Ships on-device and cloud AI (Apple Intelligence) with a privacy-emphasizing architecture; a comparatively slower-moving frontier participant but a major distribution channel via iOS.

items.name: AMD
items.detail: Nvidia's primary GPU/accelerator challenger (MI300/MI400 series, Helios racks); anchored by a large multi-year OpenAI compute deal disclosed in 2025-2026.

items.name: Broadcom
items.detail: Critical custom-silicon design partner for hyperscaler AI ASICs, including Google's TPUs and OpenAI's in-house accelerator program; a key but less consumer-visible infrastructure gatekeeper.

items.name: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)
items.detail: Sole leading-edge foundry for nearly all frontier AI chips (Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Broadcom, Google); its CoWoS packaging capacity is a binding industry-wide constraint.

items.name: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) / CAISI
items.detail: US government standards body; its AI Safety Institute was renamed the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in 2025, shifting emphasis toward standards, security, and countering foreign over-regulation rather than broad safety framing.

items.name: UK AI Security Institute (AISI)
items.detail: UK government body (formerly named the AI Safety Institute; renamed AI Security Institute in Feb 2025) that evaluates frontier models for national-security-relevant risks; publishes active technical safety research.

items.name: European AI Office
items.detail: European Commission body that both develops guidance and enforces the EU AI Act's general-purpose-AI obligations; high-risk obligations began applying broadly from August 2026.

items.name: International AI Safety Institute Network
items.detail: Coalition of national AI safety/security institutes (US, UK, EU, Japan, Canada, Australia, Singapore, Korea, and others) launched from the 2023 Bletchley Summit process to coordinate frontier-model evaluation.

items.name: OECD.AI Policy Observatory
items.detail: OECD's AI policy arm; author of the widely cited OECD AI Principles, which underpin much subsequent national and international AI governance vocabulary.

items.name: US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state regulators (e.g., California SB 53)
items.detail: The FTC is the primary US enforcement agency for AI-related consumer-protection and competition actions absent comprehensive federal AI legislation; California has become a de facto US AI regulator via state law requiring frontier-developer transparency and safety disclosures.

items.name: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC)
items.detail: China's primary AI/internet regulator, responsible for generative-AI service approvals and content/algorithm registration requirements that all Chinese labs must clear before public release.

items.name: METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research)
items.detail: Berkeley-based nonprofit that runs independent capability and dangerous-capability evaluations on frontier models pre-deployment, frequently cited in lab system cards and government assessments.

items.name: Epoch AI
items.detail: Nonprofit research group tracking compute trends, training-run scale, and model benchmarking data; a widely cited independent data source for the pace of frontier AI progress.

items.name: Apollo Research
items.detail: AI safety organization specializing in evaluating models for deceptive alignment and 'scheming' behavior; has published joint findings with OpenAI on this topic.

items.name: Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)
items.detail: The oldest dedicated AI safety research organization (est. 2000), focused on theoretical alignment and existential-risk research rather than empirical evaluation.

items.name: Center for AI Safety (CAIS)
items.detail: Nonprofit behind the widely signed 2023 'statement on AI risk' and ongoing work on benchmarks and AI policy advocacy.

items.name: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2)
items.detail: Seattle nonprofit research lab (founded by Paul Allen) producing fully open models, datasets, and benchmarks (OLMo series); a leading source of open-science alternatives to closed frontier labs.

items.name: Hugging Face
items.detail: The dominant open model/dataset hosting hub and library ecosystem (Transformers, Diffusers); functions as the de facto distribution and discovery layer for open-weight AI.

items.name: EleutherAI
items.detail: Grassroots nonprofit open-research collective (GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, Pythia, the Pile dataset); smaller-budget peer to Ai2 in the open-research ecosystem.

items.name: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) / CRFM
items.detail: Academic policy and research hub best known for the annual AI Index Report, a widely cited benchmark-of-record for industry-wide trends.

items.name: Mila – Quebec AI Institute
items.detail: Montreal-based academic AI research institute (associated with Yoshua Bengio), a leading center for deep learning research and AI-safety-adjacent policy work.

items.name: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z)
items.detail: Leading venture capital firm with a dedicated AI investment strategy; among the most active backers of foundation-model and applied-AI startups.

items.name: Sequoia Capital
items.detail: Major venture firm with sustained frontier-model and applied-AI investments; participates alongside sovereign wealth funds in mega-rounds.

items.name: Thrive Capital
items.detail: Josh Kushner's venture firm and one of OpenAI's most concentrated institutional backers across multiple funding rounds.

items.name: SoftBank Group
items.detail: Japanese conglomerate and major OpenAI investor/compute-infrastructure partner (Stargate project), representative of sovereign-scale capital entering frontier AI.

items.name: MGX / Gulf sovereign wealth funds (e.g., PIF, Mubadala)
items.detail: Sovereign wealth vehicles (UAE's MGX, Saudi PIF, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala) increasingly co-anchoring mega-rounds and compute infrastructure deals for OpenAI, xAI, and others.
